subtopic: Modulus and real part of a square
statement: Find all complex numbers $z$ such that $|z|=5$ and $\operatorname{Re}\left(z^2\right)=-7$. [5]
tips: Write $z=x+iy$ and translate the modulus and the real part of $z^2$ into two equations in $x^2$ and $y^2$.

subtopic: Powers and quotient in polar form
statement: Evaluate $\dfrac{\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)^6}{(1-i)^4}$, giving your answer as a real number. [5]
markscheme: $1+i\sqrt3=2\left(\cos\frac\pi3+i\sin\frac\pi3\right)$ [M1] $\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)^6=2^6\left(\cos2\pi+i\sin2\pi\right)=64$ [A1] $(1-i)^2=-2i$ [M1] so $(1-i)^4=(-2i)^2=-4$ [A1] answer $=\dfrac{64}{-4}=-16$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Use de Moivre for the numerator. For the denominator it is quicker to square $1-i$ once and then square again.

subtopic: A complex number whose sum with its reciprocal is 1
statement: The complex number $z$ satisfies $z+\dfrac1z=1$. (a) Find $z$ in modulus-argument form. [3] (b) Find the value of $z^3+\dfrac1{z^3}$. [2] (c) Find the value of $z^{100}+\dfrac1{z^{100}}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z^2-z+1=0$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{1\pm i\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] $z=\cos\frac\pi3\pm i\sin\frac\pi3$, that is $\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\frac\pi3\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z^3=\cos\pi\pm i\sin\pi=-1$ [M1] so $z^3+z^{-3}=-1+(-1)=-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $z^{100}+z^{-100}=2\cos\dfrac{100\pi}{3}$ [M1] $\dfrac{100\pi}{3}=33\pi+\dfrac\pi3$, so $\cos\dfrac{100\pi}{3}=\cos\left(\pi+\dfrac\pi3\right)$ [A1] $=-\dfrac12$, so the value is $-1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For $|z|=1$, $z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta$. In part (c) reduce the angle by removing multiples of $2\pi$.

subtopic: A locus given by an argument condition
statement: Find the Cartesian equation of the locus of the points $z$ in the complex plane for which $\arg\left(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\right)=\dfrac\pi2$, and describe the locus. [5]
markscheme: let $z=x+iy$; $\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=\dfrac{(x-1+iy)(x+1-iy)}{(x+1)^2+y^2}$ [M1] real part $\propto x^2-1+y^2$ [A1] the argument is $\dfrac\pi2$, so the real part is $0$ and the imaginary part is positive: $x^2+y^2=1$ [A1] imaginary part $\propto y(x+1)-y(x-1)=2y\gt0$, so $y\gt0$ [A1] the upper half of the unit circle, excluding the points $(\pm1, 0)$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. An argument of $\frac\pi2$ means the real part is zero and the imaginary part is positive.

subtopic: tan 3θ from de Moivre's theorem and the value of tan(π/12)
statement: (a) Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}$, where $t=\tan\theta$. [5] (b) Hence show that $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}$ is a root of $t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$. [2] (c) Find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos^3\theta+3i\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta-i\sin^3\theta$ [M1] equate with $\cos3\theta+i\sin3\theta$: $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$ and $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ [A1] $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{\sin3\theta}{\cos3\theta}$ [M1] divide numerator and denominator by $\cos^3\theta$ [M1] $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $3\theta=\dfrac\pi4$ gives $\tan3\theta=1$ [M1] $3t-t^3=1-3t^2$, so $t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=-1$ is a root, so $(t+1)$ is a factor [M1] $(t+1)\left(t^2-4t+1\right)=0$ [A1] $t=2\pm\sqrt3$; since $0\lt\tan\frac\pi{12}\lt\tan\frac\pi4=1$, $\tan\frac\pi{12}=2-\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Expand the cube by the binomial theorem and separate real and imaginary parts. In part (c) test $t=-1$ for a root.

subtopic: Fourth roots forming a square
statement: (a) Solve $z^4=-8+8\sqrt3\,i$, giving each root in the form $a+bi$ with $a, b$ exact. [5] (b) The four roots are the vertices of a square. Find its area. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|{-8}+8\sqrt3\,i|=16$ and $\arg=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [M1] $z=2\left[\cos\left(\frac\pi6+\frac{k\pi}2\right)+i\sin\left(\frac\pi6+\frac{k\pi}2\right)\right]$ [A1] the roots are $\sqrt3+i$, [A1] $-1+\sqrt3\,i$, [A1] $-\sqrt3-i$ and $1-\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) each vertex is $2$ from the origin, so the diagonal is $4$ [M1] area $=\dfrac{4^2}{2}=8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the right-hand side in polar form first. The four roots are equally spaced around a circle.

subtopic: Proving a modulus from a real condition
statement: The complex number $z$ is not real, and $z+\dfrac4z$ is a real number. Show that $|z|=2$. [5]
markscheme: let $z=x+iy$ with $y\ne0$; $\dfrac4z=\dfrac{4(x-iy)}{x^2+y^2}$ [M1] $\operatorname{Im}\left(z+\dfrac4z\right)=y-\dfrac{4y}{x^2+y^2}$ [A1] this equals $0$, so $y\left(1-\dfrac4{x^2+y^2}\right)=0$ [M1] since $y\ne0$, $x^2+y^2=4$ [R1] hence $|z|=2$ [AG][A1] [5 marks]
tips: Write $z=x+iy$, rationalise $4/z$, and set the imaginary part to zero. The condition that $z$ is not real lets you cancel $y$.

subtopic: Least power giving a purely imaginary number
statement: Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3+i}{1-i}\right)^n$ is purely imaginary, and write down its value for this $n$. [6]
markscheme: $\arg(\sqrt3+i)=\dfrac\pi6$ and $\arg(1-i)=-\dfrac\pi4$, so the quotient has argument $\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] its modulus is $\dfrac2{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$ [A1] need $\dfrac{5n\pi}{12}=\dfrac\pi2+k\pi$ [M1] $5n=6+12k$ [A1] $k=2$ is the first value giving an integer, so $n=6$ [A1] value $=(\sqrt2)^6\left(\cos\frac{5\pi}2+i\sin\frac{5\pi}2\right)=8i$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Find the argument of the quotient by subtracting arguments. A purely imaginary number has argument $\frac\pi2+k\pi$, so solve for the first integer $n$ that works.

subtopic: Smallest power of a quotient that is real and positive
statement: The complex number $w=\dfrac{\sqrt3+i}{1+i\sqrt3}$. (a) Find the modulus and argument of $w$. [3] (b) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $w^n$ is real and positive. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|\sqrt3+i|=2=|1+i\sqrt3|$, so $|w|=1$ [A1] $\arg(\sqrt3+i)=\dfrac\pi6$ and $\arg(1+i\sqrt3)=\dfrac\pi3$ [M1] $\arg w=-\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $w^n=\cos\left(-\dfrac{n\pi}6\right)+i\sin\left(-\dfrac{n\pi}6\right)$ [M1] need $\dfrac{n\pi}6=2k\pi$, so $n=12$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a complex number of modulus $1$, the argument of the power is $n$ times the argument.

subtopic: A quotient with a unit complex number
statement: The complex number $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, where $0\lt\theta\lt2\pi$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{1+z}{1-z}=i\cot\dfrac\theta2$. [5] (b) Hence find the value of $\theta$ for which $\dfrac{1+z}{1-z}=i\sqrt3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) multiply numerator and denominator by $e^{-i\theta/2}$ [M1] numerator: $e^{-i\theta/2}+e^{i\theta/2}=2\cos\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] denominator: $e^{-i\theta/2}-e^{i\theta/2}=-2i\sin\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] quotient $=\dfrac{2\cos\frac\theta2}{-2i\sin\frac\theta2}$ [M1] $=i\cot\dfrac\theta2$ using $\dfrac1{-i}=i$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $\cot\dfrac\theta2=\sqrt3$ [M1] with $0\lt\dfrac\theta2\lt\pi$, $\dfrac\theta2=\dfrac\pi6$, so $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write $z=e^{i\theta}$ and multiply top and bottom by $e^{-i\theta/2}$ so that both become trigonometric.

subtopic: Real and imaginary parts of an infinite geometric series
statement: (a) Explain why $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac i2\right)^n$ converges, and find its sum in the form $a+bi$. [3] (b) Hence find the exact values of $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\cos\frac{n\pi}2}{2^n}$ and $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\pi}2}{2^n}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) common ratio $\dfrac i2$ has modulus $\dfrac12\lt1$, so the series converges [R1] $S=\dfrac1{1-\frac i2}=\dfrac{2}{2-i}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{2(2+i)}5=\dfrac45+\dfrac25i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $i^n=\cos\dfrac{n\pi}2+i\sin\dfrac{n\pi}2$, so $\left(\dfrac i2\right)^n=\dfrac{\cos\frac{n\pi}2+i\sin\frac{n\pi}2}{2^n}$ [M1] equating real parts, the cosine sum is $\dfrac45$ [A1] equating imaginary parts, the sine sum is $\dfrac25$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Recognise a geometric series with a complex ratio. The real part of the sum collects the cosine terms and the imaginary part the sine terms.

subtopic: Area of the overlap of two circular discs in the complex plane
statement: The region $A$ in the complex plane is the set of $z$ satisfying both $|z|\le3$ and $|z-3|\le3$. Find the exact area of $A$. [6]
markscheme: the boundaries meet where $|z|=|z-3|$, so $\operatorname{Re}z=\dfrac32$ [M1] $y^2=9-\dfrac94$, so the intersection points are $\dfrac32\pm\dfrac{3\sqrt3}2i$ [A1] the angle subtended at each centre is $\theta$ with $\cos\dfrac\theta2=\dfrac{3/2}{3}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] area of one segment $=\dfrac12\cdot3^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}3-\sin\dfrac{2\pi}3\right)$ [M1] $=3\pi-\dfrac{9\sqrt3}4$ [A1] $A$ consists of two such segments: area $=6\pi-\dfrac{9\sqrt3}2$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Each disc has radius $3$ and the centres are $3$ apart. The overlap is two identical circular segments sharing a common chord.

subtopic: A sum of two conjugate powers in closed form
statement: (a) Show that $(1+i)^n+(1-i)^n=2^{\frac{n+2}2}\cos\dfrac{n\pi}4$ for every positive integer $n$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact value of $(1+i)^{12}+(1-i)^{12}$, and state the smallest positive integer $n$ for which the sum is $0$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1+i=\sqrt2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi4+i\sin\dfrac\pi4\right)$ and $1-i=\sqrt2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi4-i\sin\dfrac\pi4\right)$ [A1] by de Moivre, $(1\pm i)^n=2^{n/2}\left(\cos\dfrac{n\pi}4\pm i\sin\dfrac{n\pi}4\right)$ [M1] adding, the imaginary parts cancel [A1] $2\cdot2^{n/2}\cos\dfrac{n\pi}4=2^{\frac{n+2}2}\cos\dfrac{n\pi}4$ [AG][A1] [4 marks] (b) $2^7\cos3\pi=-128$ [A1] $\cos\dfrac{n\pi}4=0$ first when $n=2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The two numbers are complex conjugates, so their $n$th powers are conjugates and the sum is twice the real part.

subtopic: Parallel and series impedance
statement: In an alternating-current circuit two components have impedances $Z_1=8+6i$ ohms and $Z_2=5-12i$ ohms. When they are connected in parallel the total impedance $Z$ satisfies $\dfrac1Z=\dfrac1{Z_1}+\dfrac1{Z_2}$. (a) Find $Z$ in the form $a+bi$, giving $a$ and $b$ to three significant figures. [3] (b) A source of voltage $230$ volts is applied, so that the current is $I=\dfrac{230}Z$ amperes. Using the unrounded value of $Z$, find the amplitude of $I$ and its argument in radians, each to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Combine the reciprocals into a single fraction $\frac{Z_1Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$ and use a calculator in complex mode. For the current, $\arg(1/Z)=-\arg Z$.

subtopic: Quartic with complex roots and the quadrilateral they form
statement: The polynomial $P(z)=z^4-z^3+6z^2-z+15$ has real coefficients. (a) Use your calculator to find the four roots of $P(z)=0$, giving real and imaginary parts to three significant figures. [2] (b) In the complex plane, the four roots are the vertices of a quadrilateral. Find its area, to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1\pm2i$ [A1] $-0.5\pm1.66i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the roots form an isosceles trapezium with parallel sides along $\operatorname{Re}z=1$ and $\operatorname{Re}z=-0.5$ [R1] parallel side lengths $4$ and $2(1.6583\dots)=3.3166\dots$ [A1] distance between them $=1.5$ [A1] area $=\dfrac12(4+3.3166)(1.5)=5.49$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the polynomial solver in complex mode. Conjugate pairs give two vertical segments of different lengths, so the quadrilateral is a trapezium.

subtopic: Iterating z squared plus c until the modulus exceeds 2
statement: A sequence of complex numbers is defined by $z_0=0$ and $z_{n+1}=z_n^2+c$, where $c=0.5+0.5i$. (a) Find $z_1$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (b) Find the smallest value of $n$ for which $|z_n|\gt2$. [3]
tips: Iterate on a calculator, keeping the complex values stored in full. The sequence leaves the disc of radius $2$ after only a few steps.

subtopic: Regular heptagon formed by the seventh roots of a complex number
statement: The seven roots of $z^7=2-5i$ are the vertices of a regular heptagon in the complex plane. (a) Find the modulus of each root, to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the root with the smallest positive argument, in the form $a+bi$ with $a, b$ to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the area of the heptagon, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|z|^7=\sqrt{2^2+5^2}=\sqrt{29}$ [M1] $|z|=29^{1/14}=1.27$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\arg(2-5i)=-1.1903\dots$ so one root has argument $-0.1700\dots$ [A1] roots are spaced $\dfrac{2\pi}7$ apart, so the smallest positive argument is $-0.1700+0.8976=0.7276\dots$ [M1] $z=0.950+0.846i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the heptagon splits into $7$ triangles, each with two sides of length $R=1.2719\dots$ and included angle $\dfrac{2\pi}7$ [M1] area $=7\times\dfrac12R^2\sin\dfrac{2\pi}7$ [A1] $=4.43$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The roots are equally spaced around a circle of radius $|w|^{1/7}$, so the polygon splits into seven congruent isosceles triangles with apex at the origin.

subtopic: Greatest and least modulus and argument on a circle
statement: The complex number $z$ satisfies $|z-6-8i|=3$. (a) Find the greatest and least possible values of $|z|$. [2] (b) Find the greatest possible value of $\arg z$, in radians to three significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) the centre $6+8i$ is $10$ from the origin [M1] greatest $=13$, least $=7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) the tangent from the origin makes angle $\alpha$ with the line to the centre where $\sin\alpha=\dfrac3{10}$ [M1][A1] $\alpha=0.3047\dots$ [A1] the line to the centre has argument $\arctan\dfrac86=0.9273\dots$, so the greatest argument is $0.9273+0.3047=1.23$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The points $z$ lie on a circle of radius $3$ centred at $6+8i$. The extreme arguments occur at the two tangent lines from the origin.

subtopic: Linear map of a triangle in the complex plane
statement: The triangle $ABC$ has vertices at the complex numbers $A=1$, $B=5+i$ and $C=2+4i$. Each vertex $z$ is mapped to $w=(2+i)z-3i$, giving the triangle $A'B'C'$. (a) Find the complex numbers $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$. [3] (b) Triangle $ABC$ has area $7.5$. Find the area of $A'B'C'$. [2] (c) Find the angle through which every line segment is rotated, in radians to three significant figures. [1]
markscheme: (a) $A'=(2+i)(1)-3i=2-2i$ [A1] $B'=(2+i)(5+i)-3i=9+4i$ [A1] $C'=(2+i)(2+4i)-3i=7i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) a map $z\mapsto az+b$ multiplies lengths by $|a|=\sqrt5$ [M1] area scale factor $5$, so area $=37.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\arg(2+i)=0.464$ radians [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Multiplying by $2+i$ enlarges by $|2+i|$ and rotates by $\arg(2+i)$; adding $-3i$ only translates. Areas scale by the square of the length factor.

subtopic: Maximum of a frequency response modulus
statement: A circuit has a response $H(t)=\dfrac{1+it}{1-t^2+it}$ at frequency $t\gt0$. (a) Show that $|H(t)|^2=\dfrac{1+t^2}{t^4-t^2+1}$. [3] (b) Use your calculator to find the greatest value of $|H(t)|$ and the value of $t$ at which it occurs, each to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Use $|a+bi|^2=a^2+b^2$ for numerator and denominator separately. For part (b), enter $|H(t)|$ as a function and find its maximum.

subtopic: Damped spiral motion described by a complex exponential
statement: The position of a particle in the complex plane at time $t\ge0$ seconds is $z=3e^{(-0.2+2i)t}$. (a) Find the first time at which $|z|\lt0.5$, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the number of complete revolutions the particle has made about the origin by the time in part (a). Use the unrounded time from part (a). [2] (c) Find the first time $t\gt0$ at which $z$ is purely imaginary. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|z|=3e^{-0.2t}$ [M1] $3e^{-0.2t}=0.5$ [M1] $t=5\ln6=8.96$ seconds [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\arg z=2t$, so the angle turned is $2\times8.9588=17.9$ radians [M1] $\dfrac{17.9}{2\pi}=2.85$, so $2$ complete revolutions [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos2t=0$ [M1] $t=\dfrac\pi4=0.785$ seconds [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write $e^{(a+bi)t}=e^{at}\left(\cos bt+i\sin bt\right)$. The modulus gives the decay and the argument gives the angle turned.

subtopic: Image of a circle under w = z + 1/z
statement: The complex number $z=2\left(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\right)$ with $0\le\theta\lt2\pi$, and $w=z+\dfrac1z$. (a) Show that $w=\dfrac52\cos\theta+\dfrac32i\sin\theta$. [3] (b) Find the Cartesian equation of the curve traced by $w$ as $\theta$ varies. [2] (c) Find the area enclosed by this curve, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac1z=\dfrac12\left(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\right)$ [M1] $w=\left(2+\dfrac12\right)\cos\theta+i\left(2-\dfrac12\right)\sin\theta$ [A1] $=\dfrac52\cos\theta+\dfrac32i\sin\theta$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=\dfrac52\cos\theta$, $y=\dfrac32\sin\theta$ [M1] $\dfrac{x^2}{6.25}+\dfrac{y^2}{2.25}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) an ellipse with semi-axes $\dfrac52$ and $\dfrac32$ [M1] area $=\pi\cdot\dfrac52\cdot\dfrac32=11.8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $|z|=2$ to write $1/z$ as $\frac12(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta)$. The result is an ellipse, and an ellipse with semi-axes $a$ and $b$ has area $\pi ab$.

subtopic: Missing vertices of a square from a diagonal
statement: In the complex plane, $ABCD$ is a square labelled anticlockwise, with $A=1+2i$ and $C=5+4i$. (a) Find the complex numbers $B$ and $D$. [4] (b) Find the area of $ABCD$. [2] (c) The circle through $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ has equation $|z-p|=r$. Find $p$ and $r$. [1]
markscheme: (a) the centre is $M=\dfrac{A+C}2=3+3i$ [A1] $A-M=-2-i$ [A1] rotating by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise gives $B-M=i(-2-i)=1-2i$ [M1] $B=4+i$ and $D=2+5i$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $AC=\sqrt{4^2+2^2}=\sqrt{20}$ [M1] area $=\dfrac{AC^2}{2}=10$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $p=3+3i$, $r=\sqrt5$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The diagonals of a square bisect each other at right angles. Rotating the vector from the centre to $A$ by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise gives the vector from the centre to $B$.

subtopic: Powers of a complex number: growth and sign of the real part
statement: The sequence $z_n=(1.2+0.5i)^n$ is defined for positive integers $n$. (a) Find the modulus and argument of $1.2+0.5i$, to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the least $n$ for which $|z_n|\gt100$. [3] (c) Find the least $n$ for which $|z_n|\gt100$ and $\operatorname{Re}(z_n)\lt0$. [3]
markscheme: (a) modulus $=1.3$ [A1] argument $=0.395$ radians [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1.3^n\gt100$ [M1] $n\gt\dfrac{\ln100}{\ln1.3}=17.55\dots$ [A1] $n=18$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\operatorname{Re}(z_n)=1.3^n\cos(0.3948n)$ [M1] $\operatorname{Re}(z_{18})=76.5\gt0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(z_{19})=50.5\gt0$ [A1] $n=20$ gives $\operatorname{Re}(z_{20})=-7.95\lt0$ with $|z_{20}|=190\gt100$, so $n=20$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $|z^n|=|z|^n$ and $\arg z^n=n\arg z$. For the sign of the real part, test successive values of $n$ with the calculator.

subtopic: Real part of a finite and an infinite geometric series
statement: Let $r=0.9\left(\cos\dfrac\pi6+i\sin\dfrac\pi6\right)$. (a) Find $S_{20}=\sum_{k=0}^{19}r^k$ in the form $a+bi$, to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find $S_\infty=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}r^k$ in the form $a+bi$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) By what percentage is $\operatorname{Re}(S_{20})$ less than $\operatorname{Re}(S_\infty)$? Give your answer to the nearest percent. Use unrounded values. [2]
tips: Use the geometric series formula with a complex ratio, keeping full calculator values. The real part of $r^k$ is $0.9^k\cos\frac{k\pi}6$.

subtopic: Roots of unity, the regular pentagon and exact values
statement: This question investigates the $n$th roots of unity. Let $\omega=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}n+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}n$ where $n\ge2$. (a) Show that $1+\omega+\omega^2+\dots+\omega^{n-1}=0$. [3] (b) For $n=5$, by taking real parts show that $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5+\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5=-\dfrac12$. [2] (c) Let $x=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5$. Use the result of part (b) and a double-angle formula to show that $4x^2+2x-1=0$, and hence find $x$ in exact form. [4] (d) The five numbers $1, \omega, \omega^2, \omega^3, \omega^4$ (with $n=5$) are the vertices of a regular pentagon. Given that $z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1=\prod_{k=1}^{4}\left(z-\omega^k\right)$, find the product of the distances from the vertex at $1$ to the other four vertices. [4] (e) Given that $\left|1-\omega^k\right|=2\sin\dfrac{k\pi}5$, deduce the exact value of $\sin\dfrac\pi5\sin\dfrac{2\pi}5$. [2]
markscheme: (a) geometric series with ratio $\omega$, sum $=\dfrac{\omega^n-1}{\omega-1}$ [M1] $\omega^n=\cos2\pi+i\sin2\pi=1$ [A1] since $\omega\ne1$ the sum is $0$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) real part: $1+\cos72^\circ+\cos144^\circ+\cos216^\circ+\cos288^\circ=0$ [M1] $\cos216^\circ=\cos144^\circ$ and $\cos288^\circ=\cos72^\circ$, so $1+2\left(\cos\frac{2\pi}5+\cos\frac{4\pi}5\right)=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5=2x^2-1$ [M1] $x+2x^2-1=-\dfrac12$ [A1] so $4x^2+2x-1=0$ [AG][A1] $x=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}4$ and $x\gt0$, so $x=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}4$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) put $z=1$: $\prod_{k=1}^4\left(1-\omega^k\right)=5$ [M1][A1] the distances are $\left|1-\omega^k\right|$ [M1] their product is $\left|\prod\left(1-\omega^k\right)\right|=5$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $16\sin\frac\pi5\sin\frac{2\pi}5\sin\frac{3\pi}5\sin\frac{4\pi}5=5$ and $\sin\frac{3\pi}5=\sin\frac{2\pi}5$, $\sin\frac{4\pi}5=\sin\frac\pi5$ [M1] $\left(\sin\frac\pi5\sin\frac{2\pi}5\right)^2=\dfrac5{16}$, so the value is $\dfrac{\sqrt5}4$ since it is positive [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Part (d) uses the factorisation evaluated at $z=1$. A chord of the unit circle subtending angle $\theta$ has length $2\sin\frac\theta2$.

subtopic: Trigonometric sums by summing a complex geometric series
statement: This question uses complex numbers to sum trigonometric series. Throughout, $\theta$ is not a multiple of $2\pi$ and $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. (a) By summing a geometric series in $z$, show that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\cos k\theta=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\cos\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$. [5] (b) Write down a similar expression for $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sin k\theta$. [1] (c) Use part (a) with $n=6$ and $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}7$ to find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac\pi7+\cos\dfrac{3\pi}7+\cos\dfrac{5\pi}7$. [6] (d) For $|r|\lt1$, show that $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}r^k\cos k\theta=\dfrac{r\cos\theta-r^2}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sum_{k=1}^nz^k=\dfrac{z\left(z^n-1\right)}{z-1}$ [M1] factor $z^{n/2}$ and $z^{1/2}$: $=\dfrac{z^{(n+1)/2}\left(z^{n/2}-z^{-n/2}\right)}{z^{1/2}-z^{-1/2}}$ [A1] $z^{n/2}-z^{-n/2}=2i\sin\dfrac{n\theta}2$ and $z^{1/2}-z^{-1/2}=2i\sin\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] so the sum is $\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}\left[\cos\dfrac{(n+1)\theta}2+i\sin\dfrac{(n+1)\theta}2\right]$ [M1] real part gives the result [AG][A1] [5 marks] (b) $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sin k\theta=\dfrac{\sin\frac{n\theta}2\sin\frac{(n+1)\theta}2}{\sin\frac\theta2}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\sum_{k=1}^6\cos\dfrac{2k\pi}7=\dfrac{\sin\frac{6\pi}7\cos\pi}{\sin\frac\pi7}$ [M1] $\sin\dfrac{6\pi}7=\sin\dfrac\pi7$ and $\cos\pi=-1$, so the sum is $-1$ [A1] $\cos\dfrac{2k\pi}7=\cos\dfrac{2(7-k)\pi}7$, so $2\left(\cos\frac{2\pi}7+\cos\frac{4\pi}7+\cos\frac{6\pi}7\right)=-1$ [M1] hence $\cos\frac{2\pi}7+\cos\frac{4\pi}7+\cos\frac{6\pi}7=-\dfrac12$ [A1] $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}7=-\cos\dfrac{5\pi}7$, $\cos\dfrac{4\pi}7=-\cos\dfrac{3\pi}7$, $\cos\dfrac{6\pi}7=-\cos\dfrac\pi7$ [M1] so the required value is $\dfrac12$ [A1] [6 marks] (d) $\sum_{k=1}^\infty(rz)^k=\dfrac{rz}{1-rz}$ since $|rz|\lt1$ [M1] multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: $\dfrac{rz(1-r\overline z)}{|1-rz|^2}=\dfrac{rz-r^2}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^2}$ [A1] real part gives the result [AG][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Parts (a) and (b) are the real and imaginary parts of one complex sum. In part (c) use the symmetry $\cos\frac{2k\pi}7=\cos\frac{2(7-k)\pi}7$.

subtopic: A condition for an equilateral triangle in the complex plane
statement: This question investigates when three complex numbers $z_1$, $z_2$, $z_3$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Let $\omega=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}3+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}3$. (a) The triangle with vertices $z_1$, $z_2$, $z_3$ in anticlockwise order is equilateral. Explain why $z_3-z_1=(z_2-z_1)\left(\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right)$. [2] (b) Hence show that $z_1+\omega z_2+\omega^2z_3=0$. [3] (c) Show that $\left(z_1+\omega z_2+\omega^2z_3\right)\left(z_1+\omega^2z_2+\omega z_3\right)=z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2-z_1z_2-z_2z_3-z_3z_1$. [4] (d) Given $z_1=0$ and $z_2=4$, find the value of $z_3$ so that the triangle is equilateral and anticlockwise, in the form $a+bi$, and verify that $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2=z_1z_2+z_2z_3+z_3z_1$. [2] (e) Deduce that if $z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2=z_1z_2+z_2z_3+z_3z_1$, then $z_1$, $z_2$, $z_3$ are the vertices of an equilateral triangle (or coincide). [4]
markscheme: (a) the side $z_1z_3$ has the same length as $z_1z_2$ [R1] it is obtained by rotating $z_1z_2$ through $60^\circ$ anticlockwise about $z_1$ [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}2i=1+\omega$ [M1] since $1+\omega=-\omega^2$, $z_3-z_1=-\omega^2(z_2-z_1)$ [A1] so $z_3=\left(1+\omega^2\right)z_1-\omega^2z_2=-\omega z_1-\omega^2z_2$, that is $z_3+\omega z_1+\omega^2z_2=0$; multiplying by $\omega^2$ gives $z_1+\omega z_2+\omega^2z_3=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) expand the product [M1] coefficient of $z_1z_2$: $\omega^2+\omega=-1$ [A1] similarly the coefficients of $z_2z_3$ and $z_3z_1$ are each $-1$ [A1] coefficient of $z_1^2$ is $1$, of $z_2^2$ is $\omega^3=1$, and of $z_3^2$ is $\omega^3=1$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $z_3=4\left(\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right)=2+2\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] $z_3^2=-8+8\sqrt3\,i$, so the left side is $16-8+8\sqrt3\,i=8+8\sqrt3\,i$, and the right side is $4z_3=8+8\sqrt3\,i$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) by part (c), $\left(z_1+\omega z_2+\omega^2z_3\right)\left(z_1+\omega^2z_2+\omega z_3\right)=0$ [M1] so one factor is zero [R1] the first factor zero gives an anticlockwise equilateral triangle by the converse of part (b) [R1] the second factor zero is the same condition with $z_2$ and $z_3$ swapped, giving a clockwise equilateral triangle [R1] [4 marks]
tips: The two factors in part (c) correspond to the two orientations of an equilateral triangle, anticlockwise and clockwise.

subtopic: Coefficient in a binomial with a negative constant
statement: Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(2x-3)^7$. [3]
markscheme: general term $\binom7r(2x)^r(-3)^{7-r}$ [M1] for $x^3$, $r=3$: $\binom73\cdot2^3\cdot(-3)^4$ [M1] $=35\times8\times81=22680$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take care with the sign: the power of $-3$ is $7-r=4$, which is even.

subtopic: Constant term in (3x^2 - 1/(2x))^9
statement: Find the constant term in the expansion of $\left(3x^2-\dfrac1{2x}\right)^9$. [4]
markscheme: general term $\binom9r\left(3x^2\right)^{9-r}\left(-\dfrac1{2x}\right)^r$ [M1] power of $x$ is $18-2r-r=18-3r$, so $r=6$ [A1] term $=\binom96\cdot3^3\cdot\left(-\dfrac12\right)^6$ [M1] $=84\times27\times\dfrac1{64}=\dfrac{567}{16}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Collect the power of $x$ in the general term and set it equal to zero to find $r$.

subtopic: A coefficient in the expansion of (2 + x)^(-3/2)
statement: Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(2+x)^{-3/2}$. Give your answer in the form $\dfrac{a\sqrt2}b$. [5]
markscheme: $(2+x)^{-3/2}=2^{-3/2}\left(1+\dfrac x2\right)^{-3/2}$ [M1][A1] coefficient of $u^3$ in $(1+u)^{-3/2}$: $\dfrac{\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)\left(-\frac72\right)}{6}=-\dfrac{35}{16}$ [M1][A1] coefficient of $x^3$ $=2^{-3/2}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{35}{16}\right)\cdot\dfrac18=-\dfrac{35}{256\sqrt2}=-\dfrac{35\sqrt2}{512}$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Take out a factor so that the bracket starts with $1$, and remember that $u=\frac x2$, so the coefficient of $x^3$ gets a factor $\frac18$.

subtopic: Sum of the even-numbered binomial coefficients
statement: By evaluating $(1+x)^n$ at two suitable values of $x$, show that $\binom n0+\binom n2+\binom n4+\dots=2^{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$, and hence find the value of $\binom{10}0+\binom{10}2+\binom{10}4+\binom{10}6+\binom{10}8+\binom{10}{10}$. [5]
markscheme: put $x=1$: $2^n=\binom n0+\binom n1+\binom n2+\dots$ [M1] put $x=-1$: $0=\binom n0-\binom n1+\binom n2-\dots$ [M1] adding, $2^n=2\left[\binom n0+\binom n2+\dots\right]$ [A1] so the sum of even-numbered coefficients is $2^{n-1}$ [AG][A1] for $n=10$ the value is $2^9=512$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Add the two evaluations: the odd-numbered coefficients cancel.

subtopic: Expansion of (1 - 2x)^(-3) with its validity
statement: Find the first four terms in the expansion of $(1-2x)^{-3}$ in ascending powers of $x$, and state the values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid. [5]
tips: Use the expansion of $(1+u)^n$ for a negative integer $n$ with $u=-2x$. It is valid when $|u|\lt1$.

subtopic: Divisibility proved with the binomial theorem
statement: Use the binomial theorem to show that $3^{2n+2}-8n-9$ is divisible by $64$ for every integer $n\ge0$. [5]
markscheme: $3^{2n+2}=9^{n+1}=(1+8)^{n+1}$ [M1] $=1+(n+1)8+\binom{n+1}2 8^2+\binom{n+1}3 8^3+\dots$ [A1] every term from the third onwards contains $8^2=64$ as a factor [A1] $9^{n+1}-8n-9=1+8n+8-8n-9+64k$ [M1] $=64k$ with $k$ an integer, so it is divisible by $64$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Write $9=1+8$, expand $(1+8)^{n+1}$, and notice that all terms beyond the first two contain $64$.

subtopic: Coefficient in the product (1 + x)(1 - 2x)^(-1/2)
statement: Find the coefficient of $x^4$ in the expansion of $(1+x)(1-2x)^{-1/2}$. [6]
markscheme: $(1-2x)^{-1/2}=1+\left(-\dfrac12\right)(-2x)+\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)}{2}(-2x)^2+\dots$ [M1] $=1+x+\dfrac32x^2$ [A1] the $x^3$ term: $\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)}{6}(-2x)^3=\dfrac52x^3$ [A1] the $x^4$ term: $\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)\left(-\frac72\right)}{24}(-2x)^4=\dfrac{35}8x^4$ [A1] coefficient of $x^4$ in the product $=\dfrac{35}8+1\times\dfrac52$ [M1] $=\dfrac{55}8$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Only two products contribute to $x^4$: $1\times$ the $x^4$ term and $x\times$ the $x^3$ term of the second factor.

subtopic: Expansion of (2 - 3x)^(-2) and its range of validity
statement: Find the first three terms in the expansion of $\dfrac1{(2-3x)^2}$ in ascending powers of $x$, and state the range of $x$ for which the expansion is valid. [5]
markscheme: $(2-3x)^{-2}=\dfrac14\left(1-\dfrac{3x}2\right)^{-2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac14\left[1+(-2)\left(-\dfrac{3x}2\right)+\dfrac{(-2)(-3)}2\left(-\dfrac{3x}2\right)^2\right]$ [A1] $=\dfrac14\left[1+3x+\dfrac{27}4x^2\right]$ [A1] $=\dfrac14+\dfrac34x+\dfrac{27}{16}x^2$ [A1] valid for $\left|\dfrac{3x}2\right|\lt1$, that is $|x|\lt\dfrac23$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Factor $2$ out of the bracket so that the constant term becomes $1$, remembering $2^{-2}=\frac14$.

subtopic: Three consecutive coefficients in an arithmetic sequence
statement: In the expansion of $(1+x)^n$, where $n\ge6$, the coefficients of $x^4$, $x^5$ and $x^6$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence. Find all possible values of $n$. [6]
markscheme: $2\binom n5=\binom n4+\binom n6$ [M1] divide by $\binom n5$: $2=\dfrac5{n-4}+\dfrac{n-5}6$ [M1][A1] $12(n-4)=30+(n-4)(n-5)$ [M1] $n^2-21n+98=0$ [A1] $n=7$ or $n=14$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Use $\binom n4\Big/\binom n5=\frac5{n-4}$ and $\binom n6\Big/\binom n5=\frac{n-5}6$ to turn the condition into a quadratic in $n$.

subtopic: Sum of the coefficients of odd powers
statement: The polynomial $p(x)=(2x-1)^9$ is expanded in powers of $x$. Find the sum of the coefficients of the odd powers of $x$. [5]
markscheme: the sum of all coefficients is $p(1)=1$ [A1] $p(-1)=(-3)^9=-19683$ [A1] $p(1)-p(-1)$ gives twice the sum of the odd-power coefficients [M1] $\dfrac{1-(-19683)}2$ [A1] $=9842$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Evaluating $p(1)$ adds all coefficients while $p(-1)$ changes the signs of the odd-power ones.

subtopic: Summing a series using the expansion of (1 - x)^(-2)
statement: (a) Write down the first four terms and the general term of the expansion of $(1-x)^{-2}$, and state the values of $x$ for which it is valid. [3] (b) Hence find the exact values of $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{k+1}{3^k}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac k{3^k}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(1-x)^{-2}=1+2x+3x^2+4x^3+\dots$ [A1] general term $(k+1)x^k$ [A1] valid for $|x|\lt1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) put $x=\dfrac13$ (valid since $\left|\dfrac13\right|\lt1$): $\sum\dfrac{k+1}{3^k}=\dfrac1{(2/3)^2}=\dfrac94$ [M1][A1] $\sum\dfrac k{3^k}=\dfrac94-\sum\dfrac1{3^k}=\dfrac94-\dfrac32=\dfrac34$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Compare the series with $\sum(k+1)x^k$ at $x=\frac13$. The second sum is the first minus a geometric series.

subtopic: Bounding a power using the first terms of the expansion
statement: Without using a calculator, show that $(1.01)^{100}\gt2$. [4]
tips: Truncate the expansion after a few terms. Because every term of the expansion is positive, the truncation is smaller than the full sum.

subtopic: Integers a and b from a power of a surd
statement: Find integers $a$ and $b$ such that $\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^5=a+b\sqrt2$. [6]
markscheme: let $p=\left(\sqrt2+1\right)^5$ and $q=\left(\sqrt2-1\right)^5$ [M1] $p+q=2\left[\left(\sqrt2\right)^5+10\left(\sqrt2\right)^3+5\sqrt2\right]$ [A1] $=2\left[4\sqrt2+20\sqrt2+5\sqrt2\right]=58\sqrt2$ [A1] $p-q=2\left[5\left(\sqrt2\right)^4+10\left(\sqrt2\right)^2+1\right]=82$ [M1][A1] $p=\dfrac{58\sqrt2+82}2=41+29\sqrt2$, so $a=41$, $b=29$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: Combine $(\sqrt2+1)^5$ with $(\sqrt2-1)^5$: sums and differences keep only alternate terms of the expansion.

subtopic: Finding the index from a coefficient
statement: The coefficient of $x^5$ in the expansion of $(1+3x)^n$, where $n$ is a positive integer, is $13608$. Find the value of $n$. [4]
markscheme: coefficient of $x^5$ is $\binom n5\cdot3^5$ [M1] $\binom n5=\dfrac{13608}{243}=56$ [A1] $n=8$ [A1] $\binom n5$ is strictly increasing for $n\ge5$, so this is the only solution [R1] [4 marks]
tips: Set up $\binom n5\cdot3^5=13608$ and solve using the calculator's table, or by testing values of $n$.

subtopic: Estimating a compound interest factor with three terms
statement: An investment earns interest at $6\%$ per year compounded monthly, so that $\$1$ grows to $\left(1+\dfrac{0.06}{12}\right)^{12}$ after one year. (a) Use the first three terms of the binomial expansion of $(1+x)^{12}$ with $x=0.005$ to estimate this value. [3] (b) Find the percentage error in this estimate, given the exact value $1.005^{12}$. Give your answer to two significant figures. [2]
tips: Because $x=0.005$ is small, the terms of the expansion decrease very quickly.

subtopic: Relativistic factor approximated by a binomial series
statement: In relativity, the factor $\gamma=\left(1-u\right)^{-1/2}$ where $u=\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$ and $0\le u\lt1$. (a) Find the first three terms of the expansion of $\gamma$ in ascending powers of $u$. [2] (b) For $v=0.3c$, find the exact value of $\gamma$ and the three-term approximation, and hence find the percentage error in the approximation. Give the percentage error to two significant figures. [3] (c) The two-term approximation $1+\dfrac u2$ is more than $1\%$ below $\gamma$ when $v$ exceeds a critical value. Find $\dfrac vc$ at this critical value, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\gamma=1+\dfrac u2+\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)}{2}u^2$ [M1] $=1+\dfrac u2+\dfrac38u^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $u=0.09$ [M1] $\gamma=0.91^{-1/2}=1.04828\dots$ and the approximation is $1.0480375$ [A1] percentage error $=0.024\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $1+\dfrac u2=0.99\left(1-u\right)^{-1/2}$ [M1] $u=0.1587\dots$ so $\dfrac vc=\sqrt u=0.398$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For part (c), enter both sides as functions of $u$ on your calculator and find the intersection, then take the square root.

subtopic: Number of terms of a series needed for a given accuracy
statement: (a) The series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)x^k$ is the expansion of $(1-x)^{-2}$ for $|x|\lt1$. Find the exact value of the sum when $x=0.2$. [2] (b) Find the least number of terms of the series (starting with $k=0$) whose sum is within $0.001$ of the exact value in part (a). [3]
tips: Compute successive partial sums with the calculator and compare each with the exact value.

subtopic: Distance to the horizon approximated by a binomial series
statement: A satellite at height $h$ km above the surface of the Earth, of radius $R=6371$ km, can see a point on the horizon at distance $d=\sqrt{2Rh+h^2}$ km. (a) Show that $d=\sqrt{2Rh}\left(1+\dfrac h{2R}\right)^{1/2}$. [2] (b) Use the first two terms of the binomial expansion of the bracket to estimate $d$ for $h=400$. Give your answer to four significant figures. [2] (c) Find the percentage error in the estimate in part (b), using the exact value of $d$ and the unrounded estimate. Give your answer to two significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $d^2=2Rh\left(1+\dfrac{h}{2R}\right)$ [M1] taking the square root gives the result [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) $d\approx\sqrt{2Rh}\left(1+\dfrac h{4R}\right)$ [M1] $=2293$ km [A1] [2 marks] (c) exact $d=2292.77\dots$ and estimate $=2293.05\dots$ [M1] percentage error $=0.012\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Factor $2Rh$ out of the expression under the root. The quantity $h/(2R)$ is small, so only a couple of terms of $(1+u)^{1/2}$ are needed.

subtopic: Estimating a percentage change in orbital period
statement: The orbital period $T$ of a planet is proportional to $a^{3/2}$, where $a$ is the average distance from the Sun. The distance $a$ increases by a fraction $x$. (a) Write down the first three terms of the expansion of $(1+x)^{3/2}$. [2] (b) For a $4\%$ increase in $a$, use the three-term expansion to estimate the percentage increase in $T$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) The linear estimate $1+\dfrac32x$ is $0.01$ below the exact factor $(1+x)^{3/2}$. Find the percentage increase in $a$ for which this happens, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1+\dfrac32x+\dfrac{\frac32\cdot\frac12}2x^2$ [M1] $=1+\dfrac32x+\dfrac38x^2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=0.04$: $1+0.06+\dfrac38(0.0016)=1.0606$ [M1] percentage increase $=6.06\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) solve $(1+x)^{3/2}-1-1.5x=0.01$ [M1] $x=0.165$, so $a$ increases by $16.5\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: In part (c) use the calculator to solve the exact equation, not the three-term approximation.

subtopic: Product of two binomial series evaluated at x = 0.1
statement: (a) Find the expansion of $(1-x)^{-1/2}(1+x)^{1/3}$ up to and including the term in $x^2$. [4] (b) Use your answer with $x=0.1$ to estimate $\dfrac{\sqrt[3]{1.1}}{\sqrt{0.9}}$, and find the percentage error compared with the value from your calculator. Give the percentage error to two significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(1-x)^{-1/2}=1+\dfrac x2+\dfrac38x^2+\dots$ [A1] $(1+x)^{1/3}=1+\dfrac x3-\dfrac19x^2+\dots$ [A1] multiply and collect terms [M1] $1+\dfrac56x+\dfrac{31}{72}x^2$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) estimate $=1+\dfrac{0.5}{6}+\dfrac{31}{72}(0.01)=1.0876\dots$ [A1] exact $=1.08812\dots$ [A1] percentage error $=0.044\%$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Collect the $x^2$ terms from three products: $1\times$, $\frac x2\times\frac x3$ and $\frac38x^2\times1$ together with the $-\frac19x^2$ term.

subtopic: How far a two-term binomial estimate stays within one percent
statement: (a) Write down the first three terms of the expansion of $\sqrt{1+x}$ in ascending powers of $x$. [2] (b) The approximation $\sqrt{1+x}\approx1+\dfrac x2$ is used for $x\gt0$. Find the largest value of $x$ for which the relative error, $\dfrac{\left(1+\frac x2\right)-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1+x}}$, is at most $1\%$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1+\dfrac x2$ [A1] $-\dfrac{x^2}8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) solve $\dfrac{1+\frac x2-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1+x}}=0.01$ [M1] using the calculator [M1] $x=0.327$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The first omitted term in the expansion is of order $x^2$, so the relative error grows quickly with $x$.

subtopic: Coefficient and term value in (3 - x/2)^8
statement: (a) Find the coefficient of $x^5$ in the expansion of $\left(3-\dfrac x2\right)^8$. [3] (b) Find the value of the term in $x^5$ when $x=2$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\binom85\cdot3^3\cdot\left(-\dfrac12\right)^5$ [M1][A1] $=56\times27\times\left(-\dfrac1{32}\right)=-47.25$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $-47.25\times2^5=-1512$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The general term is $\binom8r3^{8-r}\left(-\frac12\right)^rx^r$.

subtopic: A coefficient in the expansion of (1 + 3x)^(-1/2)
statement: (a) Find the coefficient of $x^6$ in the expansion of $(1+3x)^{-1/2}$, as an exact fraction. [3] (b) State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid. [1]
markscheme: (a) term in $x^6$: $\dfrac{\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)\left(-\frac72\right)\left(-\frac92\right)\left(-\frac{11}2\right)}{6!}(3x)^6$ [M1] $=\dfrac{231}{1024}\times729$ [A1] $=\dfrac{168399}{1024}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $|3x|\lt1$, so $|x|\lt\dfrac13$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\binom{-1/2}{6}$ with $u=3x$. Both numerator and denominator can be simplified before multiplying by $3^6$.

subtopic: Sums of products of binomial coefficients
statement: This question investigates sums involving binomial coefficients $\binom nk$, for positive integers $n$. (a) By equating the coefficients of $x^n$ in $(1+x)^{2n}$ and in $(1+x)^n(1+x)^n$, show that $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}n$. [4] (b) Verify the result for $n=3$ by evaluating both sides. [2] (c) Show that $k\binom nk=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ for $1\le k\le n$, and hence show that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom nk^2=n\binom{2n-1}{n-1}$. [5] (d) Hence evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{10}k\binom{10}k^2$ and check the result of part (c) for $n=3$. [4]
markscheme: (a) coefficient of $x^n$ in $(1+x)^{2n}$ is $\binom{2n}n$ [A1] in the product, the coefficient is $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\binom n{n-k}$ [M1] $\binom n{n-k}=\binom nk$ [A1] so $\sum\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}n$ [AG][A1] [4 marks] (b) left side: $1+9+9+1=20$ [A1] right side: $\binom63=20$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $k\binom nk=k\cdot\dfrac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}=\dfrac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ [M1][A1] so $\sum k\binom nk^2=n\sum\binom{n-1}{k-1}\binom nk$ [M1] using $\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}$, $\sum_{k}\binom{n-1}{k-1}\binom n{n-k}$ is the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in $(1+x)^{n-1}(1+x)^n$ [M1] which is $\binom{2n-1}{n-1}$ [A1] [5 marks] (d) $n=10$: $10\binom{19}9$ [M1] $=10\times92378=923780$ [A1] for $n=3$: $1\cdot9+2\cdot9+3\cdot1=30$ [A1] and $3\binom52=30$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Parts (a) and (c) both compare the same coefficient in $(1+x)^m(1+x)^n=(1+x)^{m+n}$ computed in two ways.

subtopic: The series for (1 - 4x)^(-1/2) and central binomial coefficients
statement: This question explores the expansions of $(1-4x)^{-1/2}$ and $(1-4x)^{1/2}$. (a) Show that the coefficient of $x^n$ in the expansion of $(1-4x)^{-1/2}$ is $\binom{2n}n$. [5] (b) Find the expansion of $(1-4x)^{1/2}$ up to and including the term in $x^4$. [3] (c) The expansion in part (a) is valid for $|x|\lt\dfrac14$. Use it with $x=\dfrac19$ to find the exact value of $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\binom{2n}n}{9^n}$. [3] (d) By squaring the expansion in part (a), show that $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{2k}k\binom{2n-2k}{n-k}=4^n$, and verify this for $n=2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) coefficient $=\binom{-1/2}n(-4)^n$ [M1] $\binom{-1/2}n=(-1)^n\dfrac{1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots(2n-1)}{2^nn!}$ [A1] so the coefficient is $\dfrac{4^n\cdot1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)}{2^nn!}=\dfrac{2^n\cdot1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)}{n!}$ [A1] multiplying numerator and denominator by $2^nn!=2\cdot4\cdots(2n)$ [M1] gives $\dfrac{(2n)!}{n!\,n!}=\binom{2n}n$ [AG][A1] [5 marks] (b) $(1-4x)^{1/2}=1+\dfrac12(-4x)+\dfrac{\frac12\left(-\frac12\right)}2(-4x)^2+\dfrac{\frac12\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)}6(-4x)^3+\dfrac{\frac12\left(-\frac12\right)\left(-\frac32\right)\left(-\frac52\right)}{24}(-4x)^4$ [M1] $=1-2x-2x^2$ [A1] $-4x^3-10x^4$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|x|=\dfrac19\lt\dfrac14$, so the expansion is valid [R1] $\left(1-\dfrac49\right)^{-1/2}$ [M1] $=\left(\dfrac59\right)^{-1/2}=\dfrac3{\sqrt5}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\left[(1-4x)^{-1/2}\right]^2=(1-4x)^{-1}=\sum4^nx^n$ [M1][A1] the coefficient of $x^n$ in the square of the series is $\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{2k}k\binom{2n-2k}{n-k}$ [M1] hence the sum equals $4^n$ [AG] for $n=2$: $\binom00\binom42+\binom21\binom21+\binom42\binom00=6+4+6=16=4^2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: In part (a) write the coefficient as a product of odd numbers over a factorial, then multiply by the even numbers to reach $(2n)!$.

subtopic: Binomial sums with cosines using complex numbers
statement: This question uses the expansion of $\left(1+e^{i\theta}\right)^n$ to evaluate sums involving binomial coefficients. (a) Show that $1+e^{i\theta}=2\cos\dfrac\theta2\,e^{i\theta/2}$ for $-\pi\lt\theta\lt\pi$. [2] (b) By expanding $\left(1+e^{i\theta}\right)^n$ in two ways, show that $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk\cos k\theta=2^n\cos^n\dfrac\theta2\cos\dfrac{n\theta}2$. [5] (c) Verify the result of part (b) for $n=8$ and $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$ by evaluating both sides. [2] (d) Let $\omega=\cos\dfrac{2\pi}3+i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}3$. Given that $\binom n0+\binom n3+\binom n6+\dots=\dfrac13\left[2^n+(1+\omega)^n+\left(1+\omega^2\right)^n\right]$, use part (a) to find the value of $\binom{12}0+\binom{12}3+\binom{12}6+\binom{12}9+\binom{12}{12}$. [6]
markscheme: (a) $1+e^{i\theta}=e^{i\theta/2}\left(e^{-i\theta/2}+e^{i\theta/2}\right)$ [M1] $=2\cos\dfrac\theta2\,e^{i\theta/2}$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) binomial theorem: $\left(1+e^{i\theta}\right)^n=\sum\binom nke^{ik\theta}$ [M1] real part: $\sum\binom nk\cos k\theta$ [A1] from part (a), $\left(1+e^{i\theta}\right)^n=2^n\cos^n\dfrac\theta2\,e^{in\theta/2}$ [M1] real part: $2^n\cos^n\dfrac\theta2\cos\dfrac{n\theta}2$ [A1] equate real parts [AG][A1] [5 marks] (c) left side: $1-28+70-28+1=16$ [A1] right side: $2^8\left(\cos\dfrac\pi4\right)^8\cos2\pi=256\times\dfrac1{16}\times1=16$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $1+\omega=2\cos\dfrac\pi3\,e^{i\pi/3}=e^{i\pi/3}$ [M1][A1] $1+\omega^2=\overline{1+\omega}=e^{-i\pi/3}$ [A1] $(1+\omega)^{12}+\left(1+\omega^2\right)^{12}=e^{4\pi i}+e^{-4\pi i}=2$ [M1][A1] value $=\dfrac{4096+2}3=1366$ [A1] [6 marks]
tips: In part (d), apply part (a) with $\theta=\frac{2\pi}3$ to $1+\omega$ and note that $\omega^2$ is the conjugate of $\omega$.

subtopic: A quadratic in sine from a cosine squared
statement: Solve $2\cos^2x+3\sin x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. Give exact answers. [5]
markscheme: $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$ [M1] $2\sin^2x-3\sin x+1=0$ [A1] $(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-1)=0$ [M1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi6, \dfrac{5\pi}6$ [A1] $\sin x=1$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Replace $\cos^2x$ using the Pythagorean identity so that the equation is a quadratic in $\sin x$.

subtopic: Equation of the form tan 2x = 3 tan x
statement: Solve $\tan2x=3\tan x$ for $0\le x\lt\pi$. Give exact answers. [5]
markscheme: $\tan2x=\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}$ where $t=\tan x$ [M1] $2t=3t\left(1-t^2\right)$ [M1] $t\left(3t^2-1\right)=0$ [A1] $t=0$ gives $x=0$ [A1] $t=\pm\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi6, \dfrac{5\pi}6$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Do not divide by $\tan x$, because that loses the solution $\tan x=0$. Factorise instead.

subtopic: Triple angle formula for sine and a cubic equation in sine
statement: (a) Show that $\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x$. [3] (b) Hence solve $4\sin^3x-3\sin x+\dfrac12=0$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. Give exact answers. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\sin3x=\sin2x\cos x+\cos2x\sin x$ [M1] $=2\sin x\cos^2x+\left(1-2\sin^2x\right)\sin x$ [A1] $=2\sin x-2\sin^3x+\sin x-2\sin^3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) $4\sin^3x-3\sin x=-\sin3x$, so the equation is $\sin3x=\dfrac12$ [M1] $3x=\dfrac\pi6, \dfrac{5\pi}6, \dfrac{13\pi}6, \dfrac{17\pi}6$ [A1] since $0\le3x\le3\pi$ [R1] $x=\dfrac\pi{18}, \dfrac{5\pi}{18}, \dfrac{13\pi}{18}, \dfrac{17\pi}{18}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Write $3x$ as $2x+x$ for part (a). In part (b), notice the cubic is $-\sin3x$ and remember that $3x$ ranges over $[0, 3\pi]$.

subtopic: Exact value of cos(7π/12)
statement: Find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$, giving your answer with a rational denominator. [4]
markscheme: $\dfrac{7\pi}{12}=\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac\pi4$ [M1] $\cos\dfrac\pi3\cos\dfrac\pi4-\sin\dfrac\pi3\sin\dfrac\pi4$ [M1] $=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}2-\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}2$ [A1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt2-\sqrt6}4$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Split the angle into two standard angles whose sines and cosines you know exactly.

subtopic: Exact value of tan(pi/8) from a double angle formula
statement: Use the double angle formula for tangent to show that $\tan\dfrac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$. [4]
markscheme: let $t=\tan\dfrac\pi8$; $\tan\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}=1$ [M1][A1] $t^2+2t-1=0$ [M1] $t=-1\pm\sqrt2$, and $t\gt0$, so $t=\sqrt2-1$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Apply the double angle formula to $\theta=\frac\pi8$, so that $2\theta=\frac\pi4$, whose tangent is $1$.

subtopic: Greatest area of a sector with fixed perimeter
statement: A sector of a circle has radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians. Its perimeter is $20$ cm. (a) Show that the area of the sector is $A=10r-r^2$. [3] (b) Find the greatest possible area, and the value of $\theta$ at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) arc length $=r\theta$, so $2r+r\theta=20$ and $\theta=\dfrac{20-2r}{r}$ [M1][A1] $A=\dfrac12r^2\theta=\dfrac12r(20-2r)=10r-r^2$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) $A=25-(r-5)^2$ [M1] greatest area $=25\ \text{cm}^2$ at $r=5$ [A1] $\theta=\dfrac{20-10}5=2$ radians [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the perimeter to eliminate $\theta$, then complete the square or differentiate.

subtopic: Identity for (1 - cos 2x)/sin 2x and an equation
statement: (a) Show that $\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}=\tan x$. [3] (b) Hence solve $\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{\sin2x}=\sqrt3$ for $0\lt x\lt\pi$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$ and $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac{2\sin^2x}{2\sin x\cos x}=\tan x$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan x=\sqrt3$ [M1] $x=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Choose the double angle formula for $\cos2x$ that begins with $1-\dots$, namely $\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x$.

subtopic: An equation relating sin 3x and sin x
statement: Solve $\sin3x=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. Give exact answers. [5]
markscheme: $\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x$ [M1] $2\sin x-4\sin^3x=0$, so $\sin x\left(1-2\sin^2x\right)=0$ [A1] $\sin x=0$ gives $x=0, \pi, 2\pi$ [A1] $\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt2}2$ gives $x=\dfrac\pi4, \dfrac{3\pi}4$ [A1] $\sin x=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}2$ gives $x=\dfrac{5\pi}4, \dfrac{7\pi}4$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Replace $\sin3x$ using the triple angle formula and factorise rather than dividing by $\sin x$.

subtopic: Harmonic form with exact values
statement: (a) Write $3\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x$ in the form $R\sin(x+\alpha)$, where $R\gt0$ and $0\lt\alpha\lt\dfrac\pi2$. Give $R$ and $\alpha$ exactly. [3] (b) Hence solve $3\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $R\cos\alpha=3$ and $R\sin\alpha=\sqrt3$ [M1] $R=\sqrt{9+3}=2\sqrt3$ [A1] $\tan\alpha=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$, so $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi6\right)=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ [M1] $x+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi3$ or $\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6$ or $\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Expand $R\sin(x+\alpha)$ and compare coefficients of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

subtopic: Range, period and an equation for a reciprocal trigonometric model
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac4{2+\sin3x}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find the range of $f$. [2] (b) Write down the period of $f$. [1] (c) Solve $f(x)=2$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{2\pi}3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $-1\le\sin3x\le1$, so $1\le2+\sin3x\le3$ [M1] range is $\dfrac43\le f(x)\le4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $2+\sin3x=2$, so $\sin3x=0$ [M1] $3x=0, \pi, 2\pi$ [A1] $x=0, \dfrac\pi3, \dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The denominator is greatest when $\sin3x=1$, which makes $f$ smallest.

subtopic: Fourth powers of sine and cosine
statement: (a) Show that $\cos^4x-\sin^4x=\cos2x$. [2] (b) Hence solve $\cos^4x-\sin^4x=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. Give exact answers. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\cos^4x-\sin^4x=\left(\cos^2x-\sin^2x\right)\left(\cos^2x+\sin^2x\right)$ [M1] $=\cos2x\times1=\cos2x$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos2x=\sin x$, so $1-2\sin^2x=\sin x$ [M1] $2\sin^2x+\sin x-1=0$ [A1] $\sin x=\dfrac12$ or $\sin x=-1$ [A1] $x=\dfrac\pi6, \dfrac{5\pi}6, \dfrac{3\pi}2$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Factorise the difference of two squares in part (a). For part (b) choose the form of $\cos2x$ that involves only $\sin x$.

subtopic: An equation relating arcsin and arccos
statement: Find the exact value of $x$ for which $\arcsin x=2\arccos x$. [5]
markscheme: let $\theta=\arccos x$ with $0\le\theta\le\pi$, so $x=\cos\theta$ [M1] $\arcsin(\cos\theta)=\dfrac\pi2-\theta$ [A1] $\dfrac\pi2-\theta=2\theta$ [M1] $\theta=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] $x=\cos\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Introduce a single angle $\theta=\arccos x$, then use $\arcsin(\cos\theta)=\frac\pi2-\theta$.

subtopic: A cosine model for the depth of water in a harbour
statement: The depth of water $h$ metres in a harbour at time $t$ hours after midnight is modelled by $h=a\cos\bigl(b(t-c)\bigr)+d$ with $a\gt0$ and $b\gt0$. The greatest depth is $4.8$ m at $t=3.1$. The least depth is $0.6$ m. The time between consecutive greatest depths is $12.4$ hours. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. [4] (b) A boat needs at least $3.5$ m of water to enter the harbour. For $0\le t\le12.4$, find the total time for which the boat can enter. Give your answer in hours to three significant figures. [3]
tips: Use the maximum and minimum for $a$ and $d$, and the period $\frac{2\pi}b$ for $b$. For part (b) find where the curve meets the line $h=3.5$.

subtopic: Height of a rider on a Ferris wheel
statement: A Ferris wheel has radius $15$ m and its centre is $17$ m above the ground. It completes one revolution every $8$ minutes. A rider boards at the lowest point at time $t=0$ minutes. (a) Show that the height of the rider above the ground is $H(t)=17-15\cos\dfrac{\pi t}4$ metres. [2] (b) Find the first time at which the rider is at a height of $25$ m. Give your answer in minutes to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the total time in one revolution for which the rider is higher than $25$ m. Use the unrounded answer to part (b). [2]
markscheme: (a) angular speed $\dfrac{2\pi}8=\dfrac\pi4$ rad per minute [M1] at $t=0$ the height is $17-15=2$ m, the lowest point, so $H=17-15\cos\dfrac{\pi t}4$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) $17-15\cos\dfrac{\pi t}4=25$ [M1] $t=2.72$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) the heights above $25$ m are symmetric about $t=4$ [M1] time $=8-2(2.7162)=2.57$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The rider is highest at $t=4$, so the time spent above $25$ m is symmetric about that value.

subtopic: Segment equal to one third of a circle
statement: A chord of a circle of radius $r$ cuts off a minor segment. The angle that the chord subtends at the centre is $\theta$ radians, where $0\lt\theta\lt\pi$. The area of the segment equals one third of the area of the circle. (a) Show that $\theta-\sin\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}3$. [3] (b) Hence find $\theta$, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) area of segment $=\dfrac12r^2\theta-\dfrac12r^2\sin\theta$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)=\dfrac13\pi r^2$, so $\theta-\sin\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) solve with the calculator [M1] $\theta=2.61$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A minor segment is a sector minus a triangle. In part (b) solve the equation graphically or with a numerical solver.

subtopic: Solutions of a trigonometric equation over several periods
statement: (a) Solve $3\sin2x=2\cos x+1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the number of solutions of $3\sin2x=2\cos x+1$ for $0\le x\le6\pi$. [1]
markscheme: (a) sketch or solve $3\sin2x-2\cos x-1=0$ [M1] $x=0.558, 1.30$ [A1] $x=2.98, 4.59$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) the equation has period $2\pi$, so there are $3\times4=12$ solutions [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the intersection or zero finder on your calculator. Both sides have period $2\pi$.

subtopic: Sum of a sine and a phase-shifted cosine
statement: A signal is given by $y=4\sin3t+2.5\cos(3t-0.4)$, where $t\ge0$ is in seconds. (a) Express $y$ in the form $R\sin(3t+\phi)$ with $R\gt0$. Give $R$ and $\phi$ to three significant figures. [4] (b) Find the first time at which $y$ reaches its greatest value, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $2.5\cos(3t-0.4)=2.5\sin\left(3t+\dfrac\pi2-0.4\right)$ [M1] $R\cos\phi=4+2.5\cos\left(\dfrac\pi2-0.4\right)$ and $R\sin\phi=2.5\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-0.4\right)$ [A1] $R=5.48$ [A1] $\phi=0.434$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $3t+\phi=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{1.5708-0.4336}{3}=0.379$ seconds [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $\cos u=\sin\left(u+\frac\pi2\right)$ to turn the cosine into a sine, then add the two sine waves using $R\sin(3t+\phi)$.

subtopic: Viewing angle of a painting
statement: A painting hangs on a wall so that its lower edge is $2$ m and its upper edge is $3.5$ m above the eye level of a viewer. The viewer stands at a horizontal distance $x$ m from the wall. The angle subtended at the viewer's eye by the painting is $\theta$. (a) Show that $\theta=\arctan\dfrac{3.5}x-\arctan\dfrac2x$. [2] (b) Find the value of $x$ for which $\theta$ is greatest and the greatest value of $\theta$ in degrees. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) angle to the top edge is $\arctan\dfrac{3.5}x$ [A1] angle to the bottom edge is $\arctan\dfrac2x$, and $\theta$ is their difference [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) use the calculator to maximise $\theta(x)$ [M1] $x=2.65$ m [A1] $\theta=15.8^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a right-angled triangle from the eye to each edge of the painting. For part (b), plot $\theta$ against $x$ and find the maximum.

subtopic: Damped oscillation with a cosine factor
statement: The displacement of a mass is $x=6e^{-0.3t}\cos2t$ centimetres, where $t\ge0$ is the time in seconds. (a) Find the first time at which $x=0$, giving your answer in exact form. [1] (b) Find the first time at which $x=2$, to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find the least value of $x$ in the first oscillation after $t=0$, and the time at which it occurs. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos2t=0$ so $t=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) solve $6e^{-0.3t}\cos2t=2$ [M1] $t=0.581$ seconds [A1] [2 marks] (c) find the minimum of $x$ for $0.785\lt t\lt2.36$ [M1] $t=1.50$ seconds [A1] $x=-3.79$ cm [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The factor $e^{-0.3t}$ shrinks the amplitude while $\cos2t$ oscillates. Use the calculator's minimum function for part (c).

subtopic: Number of intersections of a sine curve and a line
statement: (a) Find the number of real solutions of $\sin x=0.1x$, explaining why there are no solutions with $|x|\gt10$. [3] (b) Write down the positive solutions of $\sin x=0.1x$ to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|\sin x|\le1$, so $|0.1x|\le1$ and $|x|\le10$ [R1] graph or calculator: positive solutions at $x\approx2.85, 7.07, 8.42$ [A1] with $x=0$ and the three negatives, there are $7$ solutions [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2.85$ [A1] $7.07$ and $8.42$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch $y=\sin x$ and $y=0.1x$ on the same axes. The line is an odd function, so intersections come in pairs $\pm x$ plus $x=0$.

subtopic: Daily temperature modelled by a cosine function
statement: The temperature $T$ degrees Celsius at time $t$ hours after midnight is modelled by $T=a\cos\bigl(b(t-c)\bigr)+d$ with $a\gt0$ and $b\gt0$. The highest temperature is $24^\circ$ at $t=15$ and the lowest temperature is $8^\circ$. (a) Find $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, given that the pattern repeats every $24$ hours. [4] (b) Find the number of hours in a day for which $T\gt20$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=8$ [A1] $d=16$ [A1] $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{24}=\dfrac\pi{12}$ [A1] $c=15$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $8\cos\dfrac{\pi(t-15)}{12}\gt4$, so $\cos\dfrac{\pi(t-15)}{12}\gt\dfrac12$ [M1] $|t-15|\lt4$, giving $8$ hours [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The mean value of the temperature is $d$, and the amplitude is $a$.

subtopic: Length of a belt around two pulleys
statement: A belt goes once around two circular pulleys of radii $5$ cm and $3$ cm whose centres are $20$ cm apart. The belt does not cross itself. The straight parts of the belt are tangent to both pulleys. Let $\alpha$ be the angle between each straight part and the line of centres. (a) Show that $\sin\alpha=\dfrac1{10}$ and that each straight part of the belt has length $\sqrt{396}$ cm. [2] (b) Find $\alpha$, in radians to four significant figures. [1] (c) The belt touches the larger pulley along an arc of angle $\pi+2\alpha$ and the smaller along an arc of angle $\pi-2\alpha$. Find the total length of the belt, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) drawing the radius to each tangent point and a line parallel to the tangent through the centre of the smaller pulley gives $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{5-3}{20}=\dfrac1{10}$ [A1] length $=\sqrt{20^2-(5-3)^2}=\sqrt{396}$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\alpha=\arcsin0.1=0.1002$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) large arc $=5(\pi+2\alpha)$ and small arc $=3(\pi-2\alpha)$ [A1] total $=2\sqrt{396}+5(\pi+2\alpha)+3(\pi-2\alpha)$ [M1] $=65.3$ cm [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The two straight parts are equal in length, and the belt wraps around more than half of the larger pulley and less than half of the smaller one.

subtopic: Position of the spot of a rotating beam
statement: A lighthouse beam rotates at a constant rate of one revolution every $12$ seconds. The lighthouse is $400$ m from a long straight shore. The spot of light on the shore is at distance $x=400\tan\theta$ metres from the point of the shore nearest to the lighthouse, where $\theta$ is the angle in radians between the beam and the perpendicular to the shore. At $t=0$ seconds, $\theta=0$. (a) Find the first time at which the spot is $700$ m from the nearest point. Give your answer to three significant figures. [2] (b) Find the position of the spot at $t=2.5$ seconds, to the nearest metre. [1] (c) Explain why the model gives no position for the spot at $t=3$ seconds. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{12}t$ [A1] $400\tan\dfrac{\pi t}6=700$, so $t=2.01$ seconds [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=400\tan\left(\dfrac{2.5\pi}6\right)=1493$ m [A1] [1 mark] (c) at $t=3$, $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] the beam is parallel to the shore and $\tan\dfrac\pi2$ is undefined [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The angle $\theta$ grows by $\frac{2\pi}{12}$ radians each second. The tangent function is undefined at $\frac\pi2$.

subtopic: Multiple angle formulae and the exact value of cos(π/10)
statement: This question investigates formulae for $\cos n\theta$ in terms of $c=\cos\theta$. (a) Show that $\cos2\theta=2c^2-1$ and, using a compound angle formula, that $\cos3\theta=4c^3-3c$. [3] (b) Show that $\cos(n+1)\theta+\cos(n-1)\theta=2\cos\theta\cos n\theta$. [2] (c) Hence find $\cos4\theta$ and $\cos5\theta$ as polynomials in $c$. [4] (d) Solve $\cos5\theta=0$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$, and hence state the five roots of $16x^5-20x^3+5x=0$ in terms of cosines. [3] (e) Hence find the exact value of $\cos^2\dfrac\pi{10}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1$ [A1] $\cos3\theta=\cos2\theta\cos\theta-\sin2\theta\sin\theta$ [M1] $=\left(2c^2-1\right)c-2c\left(1-c^2\right)=4c^3-3c$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\cos(n\theta\pm\theta)=\cos n\theta\cos\theta\mp\sin n\theta\sin\theta$ [M1] adding the two cases gives $2\cos n\theta\cos\theta$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos4\theta=2c\cos3\theta-\cos2\theta$ [M1] $=8c^4-8c^2+1$ [A1] $\cos5\theta=2c\cos4\theta-\cos3\theta$ [M1] $=16c^5-20c^3+5c$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $5\theta=\dfrac\pi2+k\pi$ [M1] $\theta=\dfrac\pi{10}, \dfrac{3\pi}{10}, \dfrac\pi2, \dfrac{7\pi}{10}, \dfrac{9\pi}{10}$ [A1] the roots are $x=\cos\theta$ for these values, that is $\cos\dfrac\pi{10}, \cos\dfrac{3\pi}{10}, 0, \cos\dfrac{7\pi}{10}, \cos\dfrac{9\pi}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) for $x\ne0$: $16x^4-20x^2+5=0$ [M1] $x^2=\dfrac{20\pm\sqrt{80}}{32}=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt5}8$ [A1] $\cos\dfrac\pi{10}$ is the largest root, so $\cos^2\dfrac\pi{10}=\dfrac{5+\sqrt5}8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Parts (b) and (c) give a recurrence: each $\cos(n+1)\theta$ follows from the previous two. In part (e) divide by $x$ and treat the quartic as a quadratic in $x^2$.

subtopic: Telescoping sums of inverse tangents
statement: This question investigates sums of inverse tangent functions that telescope. (a) For $a\gt b\gt0$ show that $\arctan a-\arctan b=\arctan\dfrac{a-b}{1+ab}$. [3] (b) Show that $\arctan(n+1)-\arctan n=\arctan\dfrac1{n^2+n+1}$ for $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. [2] (c) Hence find $\sum_{n=1}^{N}\arctan\dfrac1{n^2+n+1}$ in terms of $N$. [3] (d) Deduce the value of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\arctan\dfrac1{n^2+n+1}$. [2] (e) Show that $\arctan\dfrac2{n^2}=\arctan\dfrac1{n-1}-\arctan\dfrac1{n+1}$ for $n\ge2$, and hence find $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\arctan\dfrac2{n^2}$ in the form $\arctan k$. [5]
markscheme: (a) let $A=\arctan a$ and $B=\arctan b$ so $0\lt B\lt A\lt\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] $\tan(A-B)=\dfrac{a-b}{1+ab}$ [A1] since $0\lt A-B\lt\dfrac\pi2$, $A-B=\arctan\dfrac{a-b}{1+ab}$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) apply part (a) with $a=n+1$, $b=n$ [M1] $\dfrac{(n+1)-n}{1+n(n+1)}=\dfrac1{n^2+n+1}$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (c) the terms telescope [M1] $=\arctan(N+1)-\arctan1$ [A1] $=\arctan(N+1)-\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) as $N\to\infty$, $\arctan(N+1)\to\dfrac\pi2$ [M1] the sum is $\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) apply part (a) with $a=\dfrac1{n-1}$, $b=\dfrac1{n+1}$ [M1] $\dfrac{a-b}{1+ab}=\dfrac{2/(n^2-1)}{1+1/(n^2-1)}=\dfrac2{n^2}$ [A1] the terms telescope: $\sum_{n=2}^N=\arctan1+\arctan\dfrac12-\arctan\dfrac1N-\arctan\dfrac1{N+1}$ [M1][A1] as $N\to\infty$ the sum is $\dfrac\pi4+\arctan\dfrac12$; $\tan\left(\dfrac\pi4+\arctan\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac{1+\frac12}{1-\frac12}=3$, so the sum is $\arctan3$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Each part builds on part (a). To telescope, write the first few terms of the sum so that the cancelling terms are visible.

subtopic: The exact value of sin 18 degrees and the regular pentagon
statement: This question finds exact trigonometric values for $18^\circ$ and $36^\circ$. Let $s=\sin18^\circ$. (a) Explain why $\sin54^\circ=\cos36^\circ$, and hence why $\sin3\theta=\cos2\theta$ when $\theta=18^\circ$. [2] (b) Show that $4s^3-2s^2-3s+1=0$. [3] (c) Factorise the cubic and hence find $\sin18^\circ$ in exact form. [4] (d) Hence find $\cos36^\circ$ in exact form. [3] (e) A regular pentagon has side length $1$. Each diagonal and the two sides it spans form an isosceles triangle with apex angle $36^\circ$ and equal sides $d$. Show that $d=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $54^\circ+36^\circ=90^\circ$, and $\sin(90^\circ-\alpha)=\cos\alpha$ [R1] with $3\theta=54^\circ$ and $2\theta=36^\circ$, $\sin3\theta=\cos2\theta$ [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\sin3\theta=3s-4s^3$ [M1] $\cos2\theta=1-2s^2$ [M1] $3s-4s^3=1-2s^2$, which gives $4s^3-2s^2-3s+1=0$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (c) $s=1$ is a root, so $(s-1)$ is a factor [M1] $(s-1)\left(4s^2+2s-1\right)=0$ [A1] $s=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}4$ [A1] $s=1$ and the negative root are impossible since $0\lt\sin18^\circ\lt1$, so $s=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}4$ [R1] [4 marks] (d) $\cos36^\circ=1-2s^2$ [M1] $s^2=\dfrac{6-2\sqrt5}{16}$ [A1] $\cos36^\circ=1-\dfrac{6-2\sqrt5}8=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}4$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) the triangle has base $1$ and equal sides $d$, so splitting it in half gives $\dfrac12=d\sin18^\circ$ [M1] $d=\dfrac1{2s}=\dfrac2{\sqrt5-1}$ [A1] $=\dfrac{2(\sqrt5+1)}4=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$ [AG][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Because $3\times18^\circ+2\times18^\circ=90^\circ$, the sine of one angle equals the cosine of the other. The resulting equation is a cubic in $\sin18^\circ$ with an obvious root.

subtopic: Derivative of ln(sec x + tan x)
statement: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x)=\sec x$. [4]
markscheme: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x)=\dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x+\tan x)$ [M1] $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x+\tan x)=\sec x\tan x+\sec^2x$ [A1] $=\sec x(\tan x+\sec x)$ [M1] so the derivative is $\sec x$ [AG][A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the chain rule for $\ln u$, then factorise the derivative of $u=\sec x+\tan x$ so that it cancels with $u$.

subtopic: The function x^x and its minimum
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^x$ for $x\gt0$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=x^x(1+\ln x)$. [3] (b) Find the exact coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$ and determine its nature. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=x\ln x$ [M1] $\dfrac1y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\ln x+1$ [A1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^x(1+\ln x)$ [AG][A1] [3 marks] (b) $1+\ln x=0$ gives $x=e^{-1}$ [M1] $y=\left(e^{-1}\right)^{e^{-1}}=e^{-1/e}$ [A1] $f'\lt0$ for $x\lt e^{-1}$ and $f'\gt0$ for $x\gt e^{-1}$, so it is a minimum [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Take natural logarithms of both sides before differentiating. Since $x^x\gt0$, the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $1+\ln x$.

subtopic: Tangent to an implicitly defined curve
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $e^{xy}+x^2=y^2$. (a) Verify that the point $(0, 1)$ lies on $C$. [1] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $(0, 1)$. [5]
markscheme: (a) $e^0+0=1=1^2$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) differentiating implicitly: $e^{xy}\left(y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)+2x=2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ [M1][A1] at $(0, 1)$: $1\cdot(1+0)+0=2\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ [M1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac12$ [A1] tangent: $y=\dfrac12x+1$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Differentiate $e^{xy}$ with the chain rule and the product rule for $xy$.

subtopic: Growth of a balloon with a given rate of surface area
statement: The surface area of a spherical balloon increases at a constant rate of $8\pi$ cm$^2$ per second. At time $t$ the radius is $r$ cm. (a) Find the rate of increase of the radius when $r=3$. [3] (b) Find the rate of increase of the volume when $r=3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $S=4\pi r^2$ [M1] $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=8\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ [A1] $8\pi=24\pi\dfrac{dr}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=\dfrac13$ cm per second [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ [M1] $=4\pi(9)\cdot\dfrac13=12\pi$ cm$^3$ per second [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Differentiate the formula for surface area with respect to time, using the chain rule with $r$ as the intermediate variable.

subtopic: Minimum surface area of a closed cylinder
statement: A closed cylinder with radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm has volume $54\pi$ cm$^3$. Find the value of $r$ that minimises the total surface area of the cylinder, justify that it is a minimum, and find the least surface area. [7]
markscheme: $h=\dfrac{54}{r^2}$ [A1] $S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ [M1] $S=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{108\pi}r$ [A1] $\dfrac{dS}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{108\pi}{r^2}=0$ [M1] $r^3=27$, so $r=3$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2S}{dr^2}=4\pi+\dfrac{216\pi}{r^3}\gt0$, so a minimum [R1] least area $=18\pi+36\pi=54\pi$ cm$^2$ [A1] [7 marks]
tips: Use the volume to eliminate $h$, then differentiate the surface area with respect to $r$. Check the second derivative.

subtopic: A limit involving a logarithm by L'Hopital's rule
statement: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\ln(1+x)-x}{x^2}$. [5]
markscheme: numerator and denominator both tend to $0$, so L'Hopital's rule applies [R1] $\lim\dfrac{\frac1{1+x}-1}{2x}$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac{1}{1+x}-1=\dfrac{-x}{1+x}$ [M1] $=\lim\dfrac{-1}{2(1+x)}=-\dfrac12$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Check the form is $\frac00$ before applying the rule. After one application, simplify the numerator rather than differentiating again.

subtopic: Stationary points and inflection of x e^(-x^2/2)
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$. [4] (b) Show that $f''(x)=x\left(x^2-3\right)e^{-x^2/2}$, and hence determine the nature of each stationary point and the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection. [4]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=e^{-x^2/2}+x\left(-xe^{-x^2/2}\right)$ [M1] $=\left(1-x^2\right)e^{-x^2/2}$ [A1] $x=\pm1$ [A1] $\left(1, e^{-1/2}\right)$ and $\left(-1, -e^{-1/2}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $f''(x)=-2xe^{-x^2/2}+\left(1-x^2\right)\left(-x\right)e^{-x^2/2}$ [M1] $=\left(x^3-3x\right)e^{-x^2/2}$ [AG][A1] $f''(1)\lt0$ so a maximum; $f''(-1)\gt0$ so a minimum [A1] inflection where $f''=0$ with a sign change: $x=0, \pm\sqrt3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the product rule twice. Points of inflection occur where $f''$ changes sign.

subtopic: Tangent to the exponential curve through a given point
statement: The tangent to the curve $y=e^x$ at the point where $x=a$ passes through the point $(1, 0)$. Find the value of $a$ and the equation of this tangent. [5]
markscheme: gradient at $x=a$ is $e^a$ [M1] tangent: $y-e^a=e^a(x-a)$ [A1] passes through $(1, 0)$: $-e^a=e^a(1-a)$ [M1] $-1=1-a$, so $a=2$ [A1] $y=e^2(x-1)$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Write the tangent at $x=a$, substitute the coordinates $(1, 0)$ and divide by $e^a$.

subtopic: Derivative of an inverse tangent that simplifies
statement: Let $y=\arctan\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ for $-1\lt x\lt1$. Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. [5]
markscheme: let $u=x\left(1-x^2\right)^{-1/2}$; $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\dfrac{du}{dx}$ [M1] $\dfrac{du}{dx}=\left(1-x^2\right)^{-1/2}+x^2\left(1-x^2\right)^{-3/2}$ [A1] $=\left(1-x^2\right)^{-3/2}$ [A1] $1+u^2=1+\dfrac{x^2}{1-x^2}=\dfrac1{1-x^2}$ [A1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\left(1-x^2\right)\left(1-x^2\right)^{-3/2}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ [AG][A1] [5 marks]
tips: Use the derivative of $\arctan u$ and the product rule for $u$. Simplify $1+u^2$ before combining.

subtopic: A stationary point that is not a turning point
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^4-4x^3$. Find the stationary points of the graph of $f$ and determine their nature, explaining why the second derivative alone does not decide the nature of one of them. [6]
markscheme: $f'(x)=4x^3-12x^2=4x^2(x-3)$ [M1] stationary points at $x=0$ and $x=3$ [A1] $f''(x)=12x^2-24x$ [M1] $f''(3)=36\gt0$, so $x=3$ is a minimum with $f(3)=-27$ [A1] $f''(0)=0$, so the test is inconclusive [R1] $f'$ is negative on both sides of $x=0$ (no sign change), so $(0, 0)$ is a stationary point of inflection, not a maximum or minimum [R1] [6 marks]
tips: When $f''=0$ at a stationary point, look at the sign of $f'$ on either side instead.

subtopic: Greatest area of a rectangle inscribed in a semicircle
statement: A rectangle is placed so that two of its vertices lie on the diameter of a semicircle of radius $5$ and the other two vertices lie on the arc. The distance of each vertex on the diameter from the centre of the semicircle is $x$, where $0\lt x\lt5$. (a) Show that the area of the rectangle is $A=2x\sqrt{25-x^2}$. [2] (b) Find the greatest possible area of the rectangle and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) the width is $2x$ [A1] by Pythagoras the height is $\sqrt{25-x^2}$, so $A=2x\sqrt{25-x^2}$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (b) maximise $A(x)$ using the calculator [M1] $x=3.54$ [A1] $A=25.0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The vertices on the arc are at distance $5$ from the centre.

subtopic: Water filling a conical tank
statement: A conical tank has its vertex downward, height $6$ m and radius $3$ m at the top. Water flows in at a constant rate of $2$ m$^3$ per minute. When the depth of water is $h$ m, the surface has radius $\dfrac h2$ m. (a) Show that the volume of water is $V=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$. [1] (b) Find the rate at which the depth is increasing when $h=4$. Give your answer in m per minute to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the time taken to fill the tank from empty. Give your answer in minutes to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $V=\dfrac13\pi\left(\dfrac h2\right)^2h=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$ [AG][A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=\dfrac{\pi h^2}4$ [M1] $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dV/dt}{dV/dh}=\dfrac{2}{4\pi}$ [M1] $=0.159$ m per minute [A1] [3 marks] (c) capacity $=\dfrac{\pi\cdot6^3}{12}=18\pi$ [M1] time $=\dfrac{18\pi}{2}=28.3$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the chain rule $\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dt}\div\frac{dV}{dh}$.

subtopic: The quickest route for a lifeguard
statement: A lifeguard on a straight beach is $100$ m along the shore from the point $A$ nearest to a swimmer in difficulty. The swimmer is $30$ m out to sea from $A$. The lifeguard runs along the shore at $6$ m s$^{-1}$ to a point $x$ m from $A$ and then swims straight to the swimmer at $1.5$ m s$^{-1}$. (a) Show that the total time is $T(x)=\dfrac{100-x}6+\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+900}}{1.5}$ seconds. [2] (b) Find $T'(x)$ and show that the minimum time occurs when $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+900}}=\dfrac14$. [2] (c) Find the value of $x$ that minimises $T$, and the minimum time. Give your answers to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) running distance $100-x$ at $6$ m s$^{-1}$ takes $\dfrac{100-x}6$ [A1] swimming distance $\sqrt{x^2+30^2}$ at $1.5$ m s$^{-1}$ takes $\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+900}}{1.5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $T'(x)=-\dfrac16+\dfrac{x}{1.5\sqrt{x^2+900}}$ [A1] set $T'=0$: $\dfrac x{\sqrt{x^2+900}}=\dfrac{1.5}6=\dfrac14$ [AG][A1] [2 marks] (c) $16x^2=x^2+900$, so $x=\sqrt{60}=7.75$ m [A1] $T=36.0$ seconds [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Square both sides of $\frac x{\sqrt{x^2+900}}=\frac14$ to find $x$, then substitute back into $T$.

subtopic: Maximum of x cos x
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x\cos x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the greatest value of $f(x)$ and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. Give your answers to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) product rule [M1] $f'(x)=\cos x-x\sin x$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) solve $\cos x=x\sin x$, that is $x\tan x=1$ [M1] $x=0.860$ and $f=0.561$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: At the maximum, $f'(x)=0$, which can be solved with the calculator.

subtopic: Angle of elevation of a rising rocket
statement: A rocket rises vertically at a constant speed of $0.4$ km s$^{-1}$. An observer is $2$ km from the launch point on level ground, and the angle of elevation of the rocket from the observer is $\theta$. Find the rate of change of $\theta$ when the rocket is $3$ km above the ground. Give your answer in radians per second to three significant figures. [5]
markscheme: $\tan\theta=\dfrac h2$ [M1] $\sec^2\theta\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=\dfrac12\dfrac{dh}{dt}$ [A1] when $h=3$, $\sec^2\theta=1+1.5^2=3.25$ [A1] $\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=\dfrac{0.2}{3.25}$ [M1] $=0.0615$ rad per second [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Express $\tan\theta$ in terms of the height $h$, differentiate with respect to $t$ and use $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$.

subtopic: Maximum growth rate of a logistic population
statement: The population $P$ of a colony at time $t$ days is modelled by $P=\dfrac{1000}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$ for $t\ge0$. (a) Find the initial population and the value that $P$ approaches for large $t$. [2] (b) Find the time at which the population is growing fastest, and the population and growth rate at that time. Give your answers to three significant figures. [3] (c) Find the time at which the population reaches $900$, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(0)=\dfrac{1000}{10}=100$ [A1] as $t\to\infty$, $P\to1000$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) maximise $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ using the calculator [M1] $t=4.39$ days [A1] $P=500$ and $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=125$ per day [A1] [3 marks] (c) $1+9e^{-0.5t}=\dfrac{1000}{900}$ [M1] $t=8.79$ days [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The growth rate $\frac{dP}{dt}$ is greatest at the point of inflection of the graph of $P$.

subtopic: Number of real roots of a cubic depending on a constant
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the graph of $f$ in terms of $k$. [3] (b) Find the range of values of $k$ for which $f(x)=0$ has three distinct real roots. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)$ [M1] $x=1$ and $x=3$ [A1] $(1, 4+k)$ and $(3, k)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) local maximum $4+k\gt0$ and local minimum $k\lt0$ [M1] $-4\lt k\lt0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Three distinct roots require the local maximum to be above the $x$-axis and the local minimum to be below it.

subtopic: Rate of change of the distance to a point moving on a curve
statement: A point $P$ moves along the curve $y=\sqrt x$, with $x$ increasing at a constant rate of $2$ units per second. Let $d$ be the distance $OP$ from the origin $O$. Find the rate at which $d$ is increasing when $x=4$. Give your answer to three significant figures. [4]
